From July 31, 1984 to June 30, 1995 is almost eleven years (10 years, 11 months), not ten and a half; the same figure appears in contenu_vulgarise. Also, "identified by the only victim who had had the chance to see him in person" is unclear, since the entry says the second victim did not recognize him at the first trial. titre: Ronald Cotton, convicted by a face he did not have
accroche: Burlington, 1984: a victim memorizes her attacker's face so she can identify him later. She will be completely certain, and she will pick the wrong man.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the night of July 28 to 29, 1984, in Burlington, North Carolina, a man breaks a light bulb near a door, cuts a telephone line and enters the apartment of Jennifer Thompson, twenty-two. He rapes her at knifepoint. During the assault, she decides to memorize his face, his scars, his voice, so she can one day recognize him. The same night, a little farther away, another woman suffers an assault with an identical method.

## A certainty built step by step

Thompson works with the police on a composite sketch. A police officer receives a tip: Ronald Cotton, twenty-two, already known for a burglary, resembles it. She is given a lineup of six photographs, hesitates for nearly five minutes, then points to number 5: “I think this is the one.” Cotton is arrested on July 31, 1984. On August 1, she takes part in a live lineup. Cotton is in it: he is, mechanically, the only face common to the two lineups. She points to him again, and an investigator confirms that he is indeed the man chosen from the photographs. That one remark turns hesitation into certainty: each new confrontation no longer revives the memory of the attacker, but that of the face she has already chosen, which grows ever sharper.

In January 1985, an Alamance County jury convicts Cotton of rape and burglary and sentences him to life in prison plus fifty years. The second victim did not recognize him. The defense wants to present another suspect, Bobby Poole, in custody for two separate sexual assaults and whose blood type matches a trace found on the second victim: the court refuses. In January 1987, the North Carolina Supreme Court overturns the conviction over this refusal and orders a new trial.

In November 1987, Cotton is retried for both rapes; this time the second victim identifies him too, saying she had been too frightened to do so at the time. Outside the jury's presence, Poole is brought into the courtroom: both women state that he is not their attacker. The jury never sees him. Cotton is convicted a second time, to life in prison plus fifty-four years. In prison, Poole nonetheless brags to a fellow inmate that he is the perpetrator of both rapes.

## What DNA made visible

In the spring of 1995, at the defense's request, the Burlington police send the samples from both victims for DNA analysis, which had become possible since the conviction. In May 1995, the results formally exclude Cotton. The unknown profile is compared with the North Carolina DNA database: it matches Bobby Poole, already on file for other assaults. Confronted with this evidence, Poole ends up confessing. On June 30, 1995, the charges against Cotton are dropped and he leaves prison after ten and a half years of detention. On July 12, 1995, Governor James B. Hunt Jr. officially pardons him.

What this case shifts is not the reliability of Jennifer Thompson in particular, but the idea that total conviction guarantees an accurate memory: her certainty kept growing as the opportunities to see the same face multiplied, without any of them truly confronting her with the one from July 29, 1984. In April 1997, Thompson and Cotton meet for the first time, at Elon First Baptist Church; she asks whether he can forgive her, and he answers that he already had, years earlier. Together they publish in 2009 “Picking Cotton: Our Memoir of Injustice and Redemption,” and testify before the North Carolina General Assembly, which in 2007 passes a law governing eyewitness identification procedures (blind presentation, a warning that the perpetrator may be absent, the level of confidence recorded at the first identification) for offenses committed on or after March 1, 2008.

repere.texte: Mr. Cotton was arrested on July 31, 1984. [...] On June 30, 1995, the charges were vacated and dismissed. Mr. Cotton was released after spending more than 10 years in prison.

carte.punch: She was completely sure of his face. She picked the wrong man.
carte.idee: In 1984, Jennifer Thompson identifies Ronald Cotton as her rapist, with a certainty that grows at every stage of the investigation. Convicted twice, Cotton is cleared by DNA in 1995: the real culprit, Bobby Poole, had already confessed in prison.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The memoir co-written by Jennifer Thompson-Cannino and Ronald Cotton, published in 2009.
The role of eyewitness identification in DNA exonerations in the United States.

quiz.question: Why did Jennifer Thompson's certainty keep growing between the 1984 photo lineup and the 1987 trial, even though each time she picked the same innocent man?
choix: Because new physical evidence had been found between the two identification sessions
Because she had suffered a second assault that revived a memory that had been uncertain until then
Because Ronald Cotton had ended up admitting the facts to her during a confrontation
Because each identification reinforced the memory of the face already chosen, not that of the attacker
quiz.explication: Ronald Cotton was the only face common to the photo lineup and the live lineup: each confirmation from the police, starting with the simple “that's the one from the photos,” gradually replaced the memory of July 29, 1984 with that, ever sharper, of the face already picked. No new evidence supported the identification, and Cotton always denied it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What element, known as early as the first trial, already pointed to Bobby Poole as a potential suspect, even before the 1995 DNA test?
choix: His blood type, which matched a trace found on the second victim
A confession recorded by the police as soon as he was arrested for burglary
His presence at the scene confirmed by an eyewitness
A fingerprint lifted from the weapon used in the assault
quiz_supplementaire.explication: As early as the first trial, the defense wanted to present Bobby Poole, in custody for two separate sexual assaults and whose blood type matched a trace found on the second victim.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens when Bobby Poole is brought into the courtroom at the 1987 second trial?
choix: The jury formally identifies him as the attacker
He is confronted with both victims outside the jury's presence, and they state that he is not their attacker
He publicly confesses to both rapes before the court
Ronald Cotton recognizes him as a former accomplice
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Poole is brought in outside the jury's presence; both women then state that he is not their attacker, and the jury, which never sees him, convicts Cotton a second time.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the law passed by the North Carolina General Assembly in 2007 change about eyewitness identification procedures?
choix: It now bans any use of photo lineups
It requires a lawyer to be present at every identification
It establishes blind presentation and the recording of the witness's level of confidence
It abolishes live lineups in favor of systematic DNA testing
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2007 law, effective for offenses committed on or after March 1, 2008, governs identifications through blind presentation and the recording of the level of confidence at the first identification.
